new_statements.translation: STRESS. With a few exceptions, all words have the stress on the penultimate syllable, whether it is a root word or a derived word. Prefixes do not change the stress; only with the suffix noka (imperfect) does this [suffix] receive the stress. EXAMPLES. matatóeoe 'person'; belelíain 'face'; sosóloei 'ring'; poporáa 'lath game'; ngkíing 'half, other side'; fóeloein 'body hair'; takólo 'back'; tagalígoe 'nail'; hása 'to sharpen'; pangahása 'whetstone'; mése' 'to cook'; kamése' 'to make cook'; mangkamése' 'to go cook'; déle 'leave off'; kadéle 'to leave behind'; mangkadéle 'to separate'. With suffix: tóeoi 'to sit'; toeoinóka 'sat'; hána' 'to climb'; hanangnóka 'climbed'; káin 'to eat'; kainóka 'ate'.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the word, in roots and in derived (prefixed or suffixed) words alike; prefixes do not move it, and the imperfect suffix -noka takes stress on its own first syllable, which is again the penult of the suffixed word (toeoi-nóka, kain-óka). Final vowel sequences (oe-i, ai, oe-oe, aa) count as one syllable for the count (Blust 1981: 22 makes this explicit from Fortgens's marks). Dutch spelling: oe = /u/.
new_statements.exceptions: 'Op enkele uitzonderingen na' (with a few exceptions), not enumerated; the only stated deviation from root stress is the suffix -noka, which attracts stress but keeps it penultimate in the whole word.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: 'stamwoord of afgeleid woord' (root or derived word); examples are citation forms from a wordlist; p.2 adds that a/e/o vowel quality varies in open vs closed syllables and with stress, and that words are spoken very fast. Describes the Sobojo (Soboyo/Siboyo) dialect of western Taliabu, with side remarks on Kadai.
new_statements.identity_note: Fortgens 1921 describes 'Sobojo' (= Soboyo/Siboyo), the dialect of western/southern Taliabu, with comparative remarks on Kadai (eastern Taliabu; Glottolog kada1286, ISO kzd), which Fortgens says has lost even the final consonants. Glottolog files Fortgens 1921 under tali1262 and Blust 1981 treats Soboyo as the Taliabu language proper; Ridwan et al. 2020 (and, per them, Collins 1989) treat Kadai, Siboyo and Mange as three dialects of one Taliabu language, so the penultimate-stress statement is from the Siboyo dialect and has not been checked for Kadai or Mange. The tali1262 folder was cross-filed on 2026-09-17 from the kada1286 check; the same Fortgens scan serves both glottocodes.

sources.note: Nothing. Read in full: segmental correspondences among the Kadai, Siboyo and Mange dialects (vowels /e a o/, consonants /g y h t d m ng b p k r/); 'penultima position' occurs only as the environment of an /h/~/r/ correspondence. No mention of stress, accent or suprasegmentals. Confirms three dialects of one language, citing Collins (1989) for Mange as a Taliabu dialect.
